Q60763615.summary: Within a small gold disc, cloisonné enamel in green, deep red, white and blue forms the bust of Christ, his face framed by a halo marked with a cross, his hands brought before him above a green arc. The Greek letters Alpha and Omega float at either side of his head, proclaiming him the beginning and the end. Simple and bold in its gold wire outlines, this medallion is a rare early witness to enamel work in the Frankish and Saxon world.
facts: The Cleveland Museum of Art describes it as the earliest object from the Guelph Treasure, the church treasure of Brunswick Cathedral in Germany.
The museum suggests it may originally have served as a sacerdotal brooch, and attributes it to the Weser region of Germany in the late 8th century.
Cleveland bought nine pieces of the Guelph Treasure after it was exhibited in the United States in 1930–31.
Q60763615.notes: The object passed from the House of Brunswick-Lüneburg through the Goldschmidt Galleries, New York.

vam:O88811.summary: A youthful, beardless Christ sits in glory within an aureole of two overlapping circles bordered with acanthus, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a book in his left, his head ringed by a cross-nimbus. Above him are the angel of St Matthew and the eagle of St John; below, the lion of St Mark and the ox of St Luke, each with a book. The tall, narrow plaque, framed in acanthus, probably once adorned a book cover.
facts: The V&A traces the composition — Christ in Majesty surrounded by the four Evangelist symbols — to prototypes such as the mid-9th-century Majestas pages made at Tours, found in the Vivian Bible and related manuscripts.
The heavy, thick-set figure of Christ and the distinctive egg-and-acanthus border can be compared with a plaque of Christ enthroned in Berlin (V&A).
Holes at the four corners were probably for fixing it to a book cover.
vam:O88811.notes: V&A: Rhine or Meuse valley, probably 10th century; style recorded as Carolingian.
